module_title: Comparative Analysis & Transitional Provisions: Foundational Rules
introduction: This foundational level answers the most common question in Indian courts right now: 'Which law applies to my case?' It introduces the absolute cutoff date of July 1, 2024, the difference between prospective and retrospective application, and the fundamental shift in legal philosophy.

core_concepts.title: The Magic Boundary: July 1, 2024
core_concepts.description:
The BNS, BNSS, and BSA all came into force on **July 1, 2024**.
- General Rule: The new laws apply prospectively (to the future). They do not erase the past.
- Substantive Law Rule: If a crime was committed on or *before* June 30, 2024, the accused will be charged, tried, and punished under the **IPC 1860**, even if they are caught in the year 2030.
- If the crime is committed on or *after* July 1, 2024, the **BNS 2023** applies.

core_concepts.title: Prospective vs. Retrospective Application
core_concepts.description:
- Retrospective: A law that reaches back in time to change the legal consequences of past actions. (BNS is NOT retrospective for crimes).
- Prospective: A law that only applies to actions taking place after the law is enacted. (BNS is strictly prospective).

core_concepts.title: What happens to Pending Cases? (Repeal & Savings)
core_concepts.description:
Millions of cases were pending in Indian courts before July 1, 2024. 
- Do they suddenly switch to the new laws? **NO**.
- The new codes contain 'Savings Clauses' which legally 'save' the old proceedings. Any trial, appeal, or investigation that had already started before July 1, 2024, will continue under the old CrPC, IPC, and IEA until its final conclusion.

core_concepts.title: Philosophical Shift: From Punishment to Justice
core_concepts.description:
A comparative analysis reveals a core philosophical shift:
- The colonial IPC/CrPC was designed to protect the British Empire, emphasizing *punishment* and *control* (hence 'Penal Code').
- The BNS/BNSS is designed for independent India, emphasizing *justice*, *rehabilitation* (e.g., Community Service), and the integration of modern *digital technology* for speedier trials.

important_entities.name: Date of Crime vs. Date of FIR
important_entities.key_fact: The law is decided by the Date of the Crime, not when the FIR is filed.
important_entities.significance: If a theft occurred in 2023 (Date of Crime) but the victim only realizes and reports it on August 1, 2024 (Date of FIR), the police MUST register the FIR under the relevant section of the **IPC**, not the BNS.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will claim: 'The IPC, CrPC, and IEA have been completely wiped from the Indian legal system and courts will no longer use them.' This is **FALSE**. Because criminal cases take years to conclude, Indian courts and lawyers will practically be dealing with the IPC and CrPC for at least the next 1-2 decades to clear the massive backlog of older cases.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Old Crime = Old Law (IPC); Pending Trial = Old Procedure (CrPC); New Crime = New Law (BNS)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use this triangle to instantly solve scenario-based questions regarding the transition.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a scenario question gives you two dates (e.g., Crime committed in May 2024, FIR filed in September 2024), ignore the FIR date for determining the substantive offense. Base your answer purely on the **Date of the Crime**.
